name: Nutritarian diet

lead: The Nutritarian diet is a plant-focused plan built around micronutrient-dense foods such as greens, beans, onions, mushrooms, berries and seeds. People follow it for weight loss, a leaner body and better skin and health.
It comes from physician Joel Fuhrman's 2003 book Eat to Live. Published research is mostly cohort and observational work by the diet's own researchers; critics note the lack of controlled trials.

paras: Followers aim for a pound of raw and a pound of cooked vegetables a day plus beans, and limit dairy, meat, oils, juice and processed foods; a transition phase drops animal products first.
Without animal products the plan advises B12, vitamin D and omega-3 supplements. Experts such as dietitian Carolyn Williams call it a fad diet that may be hard to sustain.

angle.text: Followers use the plan to lose fat and eat more vegetables, which they expect to support a leaner body and healthier skin.

lead: The Nutritarian diet is a plant-based eating plan from physician Joel Fuhrman, described in Eat to Live (2003). Its appearance goal is mainly weight and body-composition change: fewer calories per volume of food, leaner physique and the health markers that go with it.[1]

It calls for at least a pound of raw and a pound of cooked vegetables daily, at least a cup of beans, and limits dairy, meat, snacks, juice, oils and processed foods. Fuhrman's formula H = N/C and the ANDI food ranking are central ideas.[1] Critics including Peter Lipson, David Gorski and Harriet Hall have questioned the formula, his claims and the reliance on association studies.[1]

Research includes the Nutritarian Women's Health Study, an online programme in which BMI changes were not significant overall,[2] and a cohort of 48 long-term followers who showed slower epigenetic aging and lower inflammatory indicators than 49 women on a standard American diet.[3]

paras: The plan emphasises greens, beans, onions, mushrooms, berries, nuts and seeds. Dairy and meat are excluded for an initial six weeks, after which small amounts may return. Calorie ranges are described as vegetables 30-60 percent and legumes 10-40 percent.[1]
Lipson called the health equation unquantifiable; Gorski criticised a vitalistic view of food; Hall said the diet has not been tested in controlled trials.[1]

A 2021 protocol and early results report from the Nutritarian Women's Health Study found initial BMI and waist-to-height decreases that levelled off, sometimes returning to baseline.[4] A 2025 cohort report found BMI changes were not significant, and participants found greens, beans and berries easy but mushrooms and tomatoes hard.[2] A retrospective cohort found slower epigenetic aging pace in long-term followers than in standard-diet women.[3] A secondary analysis tied higher plant-compound intake to that pattern.[5]
